newsitem.title: KENYA: Four more dead in Kenya takes toll to at least 35.
newsitem.headline: Four more dead in Kenya takes toll to at least 35.

text.p: The bodies of two missing policemen were found on Monday south of Kenya's port of Mombasa and two civilians were slashed to death, taking the death toll from six days of violence in the area to at least 35.
Police in the Indian Ocean city, already holding several opposition supporters, arrested a well-known activist in President Daniel arap Moi's ruling party.
As fears grew for Kenya's vital tourism season, an opposition-backed alliance demanding political reforms blamed Moi's advisers for stoking the violence around Mombasa.
Witnesses said a priest and a vigilante were killed in the poor Mishimoroni district on the edge of Mombasa by a band of attackers who cut them to death with machetes.
"Someone help me, someone help me," they quoted the priest as saying. The other victim was apparently killed as he went to help the priest.
Hospital sources told Reuters the bodies of two policemen were in a mortuary at Msambweni hospital in Kwale district, the site of a police hunt for attackers south of Mombasa last week.
Nine police officers are now known to have died in the violence.
The sources did not say when the bodies were brought to the hospital but Coast Police Chief Francis Gichuki told reporters on Sunday that two administration policemen were still missing.
Gichuki said police had arrested Emmanuel Maitha, a former Mombasa councillor for Moi's Kenya African National Union (KANU).

Maitha and a number of youths linked to him were held for questioning. Gichuki said they were among 33 people arrested on Monday, bringing the number of arrests to 102 since the violence erupted on August 13.
"The situation has calmed down a little bit...Our officers are still in the forest searching for these criminals," he told reporters.

Security sources said Maitha is linked to the Coast Protective Group which seeks to keep coastal land for local people. The sources said Maitha was being investigated in connection with attacks on non-coastal Kenyan settlers.
The Kenyan shilling slid to a new official low against the dollar of 70.68 as foreign investors pulled out due to worries including the unrest. But it later firmed to close at 69.99.
Sixteen suspects among 69 people arrested since last Wednesday were charged in Mombasa magistrates' court on Monday with possessing weapons including bows and arrows but no guns.
Legal sources said the fact they were not charged with murder suggested they were not ring-leaders.
Moi has blamed the trouble on opposition leaders fanning tribal hatred ahead of polls. The opposition on Monday responded by accusing government hardliners of exploiting ethnic tensions.
The National Convention Executive Council (NCEC), an opposition-backed alliance calling for reforms ahead of the elections, blamed Moi's advisers for stoking the violence.
In Nairobi, 14 opposition members of parliament separately said the government had orchestrated the violence to divert attention from calls for political and constitutional reforms.
Coast hotel staff said they began receiving cancellations on Monday, mostly from foreigners living in Kenya but also Britain and Spain. Hundreds of Kenyans fled the coast at the weekend.
In Diani beach, a tourist haven south of Mombasa, witnesses said on Monday a workshop and a kiosk were set ablaze overnight. A police, army and navy hunt has failed to stop the attacks.
The German foreign ministry warned several thousand German tourists on holiday in Kenya to stay in their hotels and take precautions as a result of the violence.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman said Bonn was not advising Germans to leave Kenya, visited by about 100,000 German citizens each year, and no violence had yet been directed at tourists.
Italy warned its tourists in Kenya to stay clear of Mombasa, the main road north and areas close to Nairobi university.
Britain warned travellers to Mombasa to remain "particularly vigilant and keep in close touch with their tour operators, hotels and local authorities."

Those Kenyans killed were mainly people from outside the coastal region. Residents pointed to leaflets warning: "The time has come for us original inhabitants of the Coast to claim what is rightly ours. We must remove these invaders from our land."
